6.0.s.en: (1) Christ, the Lord of the Sabbath

6.0.0.en: The second Sabbath: most likely the Sabbath following the feast of the Passover, and it was a day of regard among the Jews.

6.0.1.en: As Christ and His disciples were passing through the fields, they were hungry, so they took some green ears of grain and rubbed them in their hands and ate.

6.1.0.en: The Pharisees objected to the disciples because they broke the laws of the Sabbath, which were laid down by the elders of the Jews and were not the original Law, since in their interpretation of the Sabbath they forbade the process of reaping and winnowing, so the Pharisees considered plucking the ears of grain a process of reaping and rubbing them a process of winnowing. From this their attempt to catch a fault and their severity in condemning Christ and His disciples appear.

6.1.1.en: Do not look for how to condemn others, but rather seek excuses for them.

6.2.0.en: Christ answered the Pharisees with an incident recorded about David their great king (1 Sam 21:1-6), how when he was hungry he and those with him were compelled to eat of the showbread, that is, the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful to eat except for the priests, to confirm that necessity has a special status and that the Law was made for man to benefit him and not to harm him. For a person's devoting himself to spiritual work on the Sabbath day does not mean that he should fall faint with hunger when he finds no food except some ears of grain at the edges of the field, which the poor and travelers are permitted to eat.

6.2.1.en: Take care to walk by the spirit and not the letter in carrying out all the commandments, so that you may draw near to God and feel fellowship with Him.

6.3.0.en: Then He declared to them about Himself that He is the Son of Man, confirming His humanity, while He is the God who became man, the giver of the law of the Old Testament, and He is the Lord of David and the Lord of the Sabbath, who has the authority to permit in special cases small works on the Sabbath like these, as David by his authority permitted those with him to eat the showbread. This is a confirmation of His divinity and His humanity.

6.4.s.en: (2) The healing of the withered hand

6.4.0.en: Christ continued His spiritual teachings in the synagogues of the Jews on the Sabbath days, and present was a man whose right hand was withered and dry, that is, its nerves were dead. The hand signifies movement and work, especially the right, so he is a type of the Jews' inability for spiritual work, and Christ came to heal their inability. As for the Pharisees, in their wickedness they watched Christ so as to catch a fault in Him according to their thinking, namely His healing this man on the Sabbath, on which work is forbidden, since they considered healing the practice of the work of medicine, which is forbidden to the physician on the Sabbath day.

6.5.0.en: Because Christ is God, He knew the thoughts of the Pharisees without their declaring them. And Christ was not afraid of their wickedness, but boldly took the initiative to do good by setting the sick man in the midst of the synagogue to show his weakness and his need of healing, but the hard hearts of the Pharisees were not moved to sympathy for him.

6.5.1.en: Do you hasten to do good however much the wicked oppose you? Be confident that good is stronger than evil, and continue in it so that you do not waste your effort in being disturbed by the evils of others or repaying their evil with evil.

6.6.0.en: Christ reasoned with the Pharisees to guide them to the truth, asking what is fitting for the day of the Lord in their view, which is the Sabbath: to do good, that is, healing this sick man, or to do evil, which is their malicious thinking by which they try to find an accusation against Him.

6.6.1.en: And by healing the sick man Christ means saving his soul and not only healing him, for when he is healed he believes and thanks God and begins to do good by moving his hand, but if He left him and did not heal him, he would remain in his bodily weakness and not know Christ, in whom he finds his salvation.

6.7.0.en: Jesus looked at them, awaiting an answer, but all were silent, unable to reply, then He commanded and the sick man was healed. This is considered a miracle of creation, for He created living nerves, and the withered hand was changed into a normal hand able to work.

6.8.0.en: Despite the clarity of the miracle, which calls all to glorify God, evil dominated the hearts of the Pharisees, so in ignorance they sought how to get rid of Christ.

6.8.1.en: When evil fills a person's heart it drives him to harm others, and while he thinks himself wise he is in the utmost ignorance. So if your heart is troubled and you become angry, stop to repent first before you do anything.

6.9.0.en: Christ's love of retreat and prayer appears here, for He went up the mountain alone to get away from people and enjoy prayer. As a man He needed prayer as He needed food, for He is not only God but also man at one and the same time.

6.9.1.en: His going up the mountain signifies rising above earthly things and thinking of heavenly things. The Church took the rite of keeping vigil all night from Christ, as in the Midnight Praise and the night of the Saturday of Light and in the ordination of the priestly ranks and of monks.

6.10.0.en: After praying all night, the day began and He met His disciples, who were many, and He chose from them twelve to be disciples especially His own more than the rest, and called them Apostles because He would send them into the world to preach His salvation.

6.10.1.en: Christ's concern for prayer before important works and great decisions is clear here, to be a rule for us in our lives, that we take no important decision except after a sufficient period of prayer.

6.10.2.en: The way of the call to service also appears: it must be from God Himself and not from the person himself; that is, the Church chooses her servants and no one calls himself a servant of his own accord.

6.11.0.en: It is noticeable in the calling of the Twelve that He called them two by two, and the number two shows the importance of partnership and cooperation in service. He changed the names of some of them, and in general their names have beautiful meanings, namely: James = the persevering; John = God is gracious; Andrew = the brave.

6.11.2.en: Philip = the mouth of the lamp, that is, the enlightener. Bartholomew (called Nathanael in Jn = 1), son of Harith, that is, the one who goes deep. Thomas = the twin, that is, the one who clings. Simon = the one who hears.

6.11.4.en: Judas the brother of James, son of Alphaeus (also called Thaddaeus) = he who praises and gives thanks.

6.11.5.en: Iscariot = a title meaning "a man from Kerioth," the village in which Judas the traitor grew up

6.12.0.en: After appointing His disciples He came down from the mountain to a plain, which was probably the foot of the mountain; for Christ comes down to our weakness to raise us up to Himself, and around Him were three groups:

6.12.1.en: 1- His disciples, including the Twelve and the rest, from whom He afterward chose seventy apostles.

6.12.2.en: 2- A multitude of those who loved to hear His teachings.

6.12.3.en: 3- Many of the sick and their acquaintances, and also those with unclean spirits.

6.12.4.en: It is noticeable that those gathered around Him were Jews and Gentiles (the coast of Tyre and Sidon), for Christ came for the salvation of the whole world.

6.12.5.en: And He taught them many teachings and then healed their sick. The healing of diseases was out of His tenderness and to draw them to faith. But sadly, many even until now have a utilitarian relationship with God, based on benefiting from His power in healing their diseases and meeting their needs.

6.12.6.en: May your relationship with God be built on your love and your sonship to Him, and likewise your friendship with the saints, so that you imitate them, and not merely on meeting your needs and solving your problems.

6.13.0.en: The healing of the sick took place by Christ's touching them, and a power went out and healed them; and He was not content merely to command their healing, because they are human beings and need something tangible accompanying the spiritual work. For this reason God placed for us in the Church the holy Sacraments, which are the work of the Holy Spirit under a tangible form, because we are in the body and need spiritual things through a material form.

6.14.0.en: This is the most famous of Christ's sermons, which Matthew the Evangelist mentioned in (Mt 5-7) in greater detail. Luke directs it to the disciples, but it is addressed to all the believers.

6.14.1.en: The word "blessed" means happiness or felicity. And the one who receives this happiness is the one whom people think far from it because of his weak appearance. The first of these blessed groups are the poor, whom Matthew describes as the poor in spirit, that is, the humble, and because of their humility God's mercies overflow upon them and He grants them His heavenly Kingdom, whose happiness cannot be expressed.

6.15.0.en: The hungry are those who long for righteousness and a good life; these God satisfies with the knowledge of Him and fellowship with Him, so that they are filled with every virtue.

6.15.1.en: Those who weep are those who weep over their sins, that is, the repentant; these God forgives their sins so that they receive true joy, and they laugh from their hearts, that is, they rejoice.

6.16.0.en: Enduring people's hatred, rejection, reproach and false accusation of evil against us, God rewards with heavenly joys. And we are not troubled, because in every age the devil stirs up the wicked against the children of God, as the Jews used to do with the prophets of God in the Old Testament, beating them and reviling them and even killing them. Humble yourself, remembering your sins in repentance, and your longings for God will be stirred, and then you will make light of every pain for His sake, looking to the glories of eternity, confident of His help and His consolation of your heart.

6.17.0.en: What is meant here are the rich who rely on their wealth and are attached to it, for they have received their pleasure in these passing material things, and have no share in the glories of heaven because they neglected them.

6.18.0.en: Those immersed in the lusts of the world will hunger in eternity for the enjoyment of God and will not find it. And those who play in the laughter and mockery of this world, reckless and plunged in sins, will regret in the end when they are cast into Hell with unending sorrow.

6.19.0.en: After speaking in the preceding woes to the crowds, which include the Pharisees and all those far from the knowledge of God, He directs His speech here to His disciples and all who believe in Him, warning them of the sin of loving praise, because it necessarily requires hypocrisy to please everyone and obtain their praise, as the false prophets in the Old Testament gave false reports according to the wish of the hearers in order to obtain their praise and gifts.

6.19.1.en: May you have a pure conscience, so that you declare the voice of God to those around you, seeking the glory of God and not your personal comfort.

6.20.0.en: Christ presents the essential characteristic of Christians, which is love for everyone, even enemies and those who wrong us. It is not limited to a heart open to others, but goes beyond it to positive acts, whether before God, such as prayer, or before enemies, such as blessing them with kind words, or offering them deeds of goodness and kindness. For we feel that the one who hates us is a beloved brother who has been subjected to pressures from the devil, and by our love we help him, and he returns to his natural state, that is, he loves us.

6.20.1.en: Have compassion on the one who wrongs you, and offer him love, even if at the very least a prayer for him.

6.21.0.en: Christ presents practical examples of love for those who wrong us, such as forgiveness and enduring insults from one who assaults us with blows and insult. Then giving to the one who seizes our money, so we do not limit ourselves to leaving what he seized but also give him more love, such as giving the coat and not only leaving the cloak that was seized. In sum: considering everyone to be in need and giving to all, for the extortioner and the enemy need our love, and we give him more than he asks because we are not attached to material things, and we care about winning souls by love.

6.22.0.en: To make it easier for the hearers, who felt the difficulty of this love, He said to them: you wish that people would treat you with self-giving love, so take the initiative with it toward them.

6.22.1.en: Think, in every dealing with others, if you were in their place, how would you want them to treat you?

6.23.0.en: Christ presents here a truth, which is that the natural thing is for a person to love his friends and loved ones who love him, and this is also what sinners do. And lending to others and getting everything back from them is also a matter that does not exceed natural human dealing, but Christ presents true love, which is higher than human love ... love of enemies and those who wrong us, and by this we prove that we are children of God, who is love.

6.24.0.en: If we are children of God in love, we imitate Him in His kindness and mercy toward those who murmur against Him. So we offer mercy to all like God our Father, and look with a spirit of fatherhood and motherhood at all around us however much they are against us. Meditate on God's mercy to you in your past life, and this will drive you to do mercy with everyone.

6.25.0.en: Christ encourages us to love by the blessings that we receive from it: if we forgive others and pardon them, God will forgive us, and if we give material and spiritual gifts, God will give us more. He compares God's overflowing gifts to the measure of grain that was used in ancient times, and this measure is characterized by being good, with no excess at its bottom so that it holds as much as possible, and pressed down, that is, the grains are pressed within it so that the greatest amount is put in it, and likewise shaken together to fill all the inner gaps, and running over, that is, if any amount is put on it, it falls off because it is completely full. Then the person receives these grains in his garment, so that they come into his bosom. To the extent that we give generously, God gives us even more generously.

6.25.1.en: And on the other side, if we wrong others by condemning and judging them, we shall also be condemned and judged. Your giving to others shows the extent of your love for them and your detachment from love of material things and your appreciation of God's love for you, and these three drive you to generous giving. And if you possess love and giving, you will keep away from condemning even if you notice the faults of others; you will look for what you can offer them.

6.26.0.en: He continues His warning to us against judging, alerting us to the multitude of our sins that blind our sight. And while we are blind, trying to judge others and lead them on the way of life, we have nothing before us but that we and they fall into the pit of problems and greater errors.

6.26.1.en: On the other hand, we ought to imitate our good teacher Jesus Christ, who went about doing good and did not condemn others, even the woman caught in adultery He did not condemn. And the perfection we strive for is to imitate Christ our teacher in love and in not judging.

6.27.0.en: And in mockery of the one who judges, Christ makes clear that the sin of any person is like a mote or a small straw, but the sin of judging is like a beam. And He asks whether it is possible for a person with a beam in his eye to take a mote out of his brother's eye? ... Of course not, but wisdom says: let me first cast the beam out of my own eye, by repenting of judging, and let love take its place, by which I help others to be rid of their sins, that is, the mote in their eye.

6.28.0.en: At the end of Christ's sermon, He stressed the importance of carrying out His commandments and not merely hearing them, or speaking with Him with many requests such as the healing of diseases and the casting out of demons. For practical love is the foundation on which the whole of life is built, and it is what confirms our sonship to God and our conviction of His word.

6.29.0.en: He gives a practical comparison, which is that a man dug until he reached the rock, and laid the foundation on it and raised a building, so that it is strong. And another building was raised on the earth, which is sand or weak dust easily moved, so when the winds blew and the water of the river rushed like a flood and struck these two houses, the building on the rock was not affected, but the building without a foundation on the earth collapsed and fell. Likewise whoever carries out God's commandments and lives practically by love will not be shaken by the winds of trials and the devil's wars, but the other falls into sins and his end is eternal destruction.

6.29.1.en: Let love be in your heart before you speak or do anything, for it is the only aim in our relationship with others, that we may win their souls for Christ, because God is love and on Him we build all our actions.

6.29.2.en: The centurion's servant, the son of the widow of Nain, the talk about the Baptist, the sinful woman in the Pharisee's house
